USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Stay the course at the negotiating table and press to close a deal now that leverage is maximized, while holding the scheduled List 3 increase from 10% to 25% in reserve as an explicit stick rather than exercising it. Signal readiness to finalize at the proposed leaders' summit, but do not trade away the enforcement mechanism or any tariff relief before Beijing puts concrete, verifiable purchase and structural commitments in writing. Use the summit as the venue to bank China's goodwill gestures (soybean purchases, currency agreement, financial-services opening) into a binding, enforceable framework.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat reading is mildly net-negative (opportunity tilt) because every macro and negotiation data point says the US holds the stronger hand and the trade book is not yet costing the US economy. US financial conditions are benign and stable—10Y Treasury at 2.52%, Baa credit spreads tight at 4.75%, consumer sentiment recovered to 97.2, VIX suppressed, and WTI back to $62 (country_health). The dispute has not produced a US slowdown; if anything the December 2018 equities/VIX scare has been fully unwound. The timeline shows consistent US-side momentum: G20 truce (12/1), three negotiated delays of the 25% hike (1/1, 2/24, and passing 3/1 without action), and intensive Washington talks as of 4/3 with both sides reporting progress on text including enforcement language—Liu He calling a deal 'very likely.' Meanwhile Beijing keeps paying real economic costs: soybean export commitments to China collapsed to 4.3M tons versus 24.5M a year earlier, and its goodwill purchases are a fraction of historical run-rate. On the action axis, de-escalation-by-default is wrong (that would squander leverage), but escalation-by-default is also wrong: hiking to 25% now would raise US farming's $8B in unsold inventory exposure, invite full-bore retaliation, and spook the very equity-market calm that makes the White House's position credible. Hence 'negotiate' at +0.15—competitive-pressure posture, maximum flexibility, no new unilateral concessions, and let China's disclosed concessions (currency notification, soybeans, market access) become the floor of the final package. Tail risk to monitor rather than pre-empt: if talks collapse, the 25% tariff snap and retaliation would hit exactly when growth and rate signals (yield-curve flattening from 10Y 3.22% to 2.52%) have thinned the economy's margin for error.
key_factors: US macro resilient through the dispute: 10Y at 2.52%, Baa 4.75%, UMich consumer sentiment 97.2, VIX low, WTI $62 — no trade-war recession visible in the data

US holds credible tariff leverage: ~$250B of Chinese imports covered by Section 301 with the 10%→25% List 3 hike preserved as a threat that has already been delayed three times (timeline: 1/1, 2/24, 3/1)
China is the one making concessions: goodwill soybean purchases (~6.5M t vs 24.5M t prior-year commitments), currency non-manipulation agreement with notification duties, financial-services opening
US domestic costs are real but contained: ~$8B unsold soybean inventory and WTO suits/uncertainty pressuring farms, but no broad GDP or labor-market damage yet

Talks at a hand-off moment: intensive Washington round completed 4/3 with both sides citing progress on enforcement text and a leaders' summit floated — bad time to either tip to 25% or give ground unilaterally

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Stay the course in the ongoing Washington/Beijing talks and push to convert the frozen-tariff truce into a durable deal, without conceding irreversible structural concessions or surrendering on the Huawei/Meng matter. Do not escalate — a new tariff hike or hardline response would invite the US to re-impose the pending 25% tariff on $200B of our exports. Hold firm at the table, leverage the mutual desire for a deal (including the possibility of a Trump-Xi summit), and seek to lock in the purchase commitments and tariff relief already on the table.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is real but not existential. US Section 301 tariffs already cover roughly $250B of our exports, and the pain is visible in the real economy: our exports to the US fell 14.1% in Jan-Feb 2019 and total exports slipped 4.6%, with the government cutting its growth target to 6% and the Premier warning of a 'graver and more complicated environment.' On top of the tariff drag, the US DOJ charges against Huawei and Meng Wanzhou, the extradition request, and the risk of a Huawei entity-list/executive order constitute firm-level targeting of a tech champion — pushing the reading toward the +0.5 anchor. However, this is tempered by a decidedly de-escalatory trajectory: the 90-day deadline passed March 1 without a tariff hike, the List 3 increase to 25% was delayed (Feb 24), and April 3 talks produced progress on text and enforcement language. That both sides are still negotiating, and Trump has publicly signaled willingness to intervene in the Huawei case for a deal, gives us real leverage. Consequently a moderate-positive threat score (~+0.4) is warranted, and a negotiating stance (small positive action score) is right: we should not escalate (too dangerous — it would trigger the 25% hike), nor fully concede (that would gut Made in China 2025 and our tech autonomy). De-escalation-by-negotiation maximizes our hand while the truce holds.
key_factors: US tariffs covering ~$250B of Chinese goods at 10-25%; China exports to US down 14.1% in Jan-Feb 2019
Truce holding: 25% hike on $200B delayed (Feb 24) and 90-day deadline passed Mar 1 without increase
DOJ charges/extradition request for Meng Wanzhou and potential Huawei entity-list = firm-level targeting of tech champion
China GDP growth target cut to 6%; Premier Li warns of graver, more complicated environment
Trump signaled willingness to intervene in Huawei case for a deal; possible Trump-Xi summit
April 3 talks made progress on text and enforcement language with no final deal
Escalating risks triggering the pending 25% tariff on $200B of exports

sources_cited.excerpt: Intensive Washington talks between US and Chinese negotiators; both sides report progress on text, including enforcement language. No final deal signed.
Trump tweets talks made substantial progress and further delays the scheduled List 3 hike from 10% to 25%.
List 3 takes effect at 10%... Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
US DOJ unseals fraud and sanctions-related charges against Huawei and Meng; US formally requests Meng's extradition from Canada.
Exports to the United States fell 14.1% from a year earlier to $52.3 billion in the first two months of 2019. China's global exports sank 4.6% to $353.2 billion.
Growth targets have been slashed... government set a target of just 6% GDP growth. Premier Li: economy has encountered new downward pressure.
Trump: 'I would certainly intervene' in the Huawei CFO's case if it helped win a trade deal.
Trump suggested criminal charges against Huawei could be used as a bargaining chip... considering an executive order that would impose harsh penalties on Huawei.
